title: The swollen eyelid that hurts to move
stem: A 13-year-old boy has three days of worsening left eyelid swelling and frontal headache, after a week of purulent nasal discharge. Temperature 38.4 °C. BVA 20/20 OD, 20/40 OS. Mild left RAPD, red saturation 60% OS, 3 mm proptosis, tense chemosis, painful restriction of elevation and abduction. IOP 17 OD, 27 OS. Cornea clear, chamber quiet, fundus normal.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Preseptal cellulitis with reactive chemosis
Idiopathic orbital inflammatory syndrome
Cavernous sinus thrombosis complicating sinusitis
Orbital cellulitis of ethmoid sinus origin
Orbital rhabdomyosarcoma with secondary inflammation

items.why: Proptosis, painful restricted motility, RAPD, reduced colour and acuity, and raised IOP all place the disease behind the septum. Fever with a week of purulent rhinorrhoea names the source.

dis.label: Cavernous sinus thrombosis
dis.tempting: The correct escalation of this infection, and it also gives proptosis and chemosis.
dis.ruled: Signs stay strictly unilateral, with no multiple cranial neuropathy and no V1-V2 loss.

dis.label: Preseptal cellulitis
dis.tempting: The visible finding is a swollen lid, and preseptal disease is commoner at this age.
dis.ruled: Preseptal disease spares acuity, pupil, colour, motility and globe position.

dis.label: Rhabdomyosarcoma
dis.tempting: Rapid proptosis in a child is the classic teaching phrase for it.
dis.ruled: Fever and purulent sinus disease over three days fit infection, not tumour.

items.q: Which three findings measure optic nerve function, rather than supporting the infective diagnosis?

options.t: Temperature 38.4 °C
Left relative afferent pupillary defect
Red saturation reduced to 60% OS
Purulent nasal discharge for one week
Intraocular pressure 27 mmHg OS
Best corrected acuity 20/40 OS

items.why: The item asks for afferent function, not for evidence of infection. An RAPD, dyschromatopsia and reduced best acuity each measure optic nerve conduction directly.

dis.label: IOP 27 mmHg
dis.tempting: It is genuinely abnormal, and orbital pressure is what threatens the nerve.
dis.ruled: It measures orbital pressure, not conduction. Normalising it proves nothing.

dis.label: Fever, purulent discharge
dis.tempting: They confirm infection and drive the diagnosis.
dis.ruled: Neither measures the eye. A febrile child can have a normal afferent system.

items.q: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.t: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate, nasal decongestant, review in 24 hours
Same-day referral for contrast CT, intravenous antibiotics, ophthalmology and ENT
Outpatient MRI within 48 hours, then decide about admission
Intravenous antibiotics booked for the morning, oral cover overnight
Oral corticosteroid with a topical antibiotic to settle the swelling

items.short: Same-day referral, contrast CT, IV antibiotics
items.why: Orbital cellulitis with afferent dysfunction threatens the eye and, through intracranial extension, life. Imaging, intravenous therapy and surgical availability are arranged together, today.

dis.label: IV antibiotics tomorrow
dis.tempting: It sees that intravenous therapy is needed and feels like a fair compromise.
dis.ruled: The overnight delay is where vision goes. The decision point is the RAPD, now.

dis.label: Outpatient MRI in 48 hours
dis.tempting: MRI is the better soft-tissue study, so it reads as the more thorough answer.
dis.ruled: Contrast CT answers today's questions faster: sinus, collection, apex, bone.

items.q: Which anatomic route most commonly explains this presentation?

options.t: Direct spread across the lamina papyracea from the ethmoid sinus
Retrograde thrombophlebitis through valveless facial and orbital veins
Extension through the optic canal from the sphenoid sinus
Ascending infection along the nasolacrimal duct from the inferior meatus
Haematogenous seeding of the orbit from an occult bacteraemia

items.why: The medial orbital wall is paper-thin and perforated by vessels, which makes contiguous ethmoid spread the usual route and explains why abduction and elevation fail first.

dis.label: Valveless venous spread
dis.tempting: A real mechanism, and how mid-face infection reaches the cavernous sinus.
dis.ruled: Not the usual route from sinusitis, and it does not localise medially.

dis.label: Optic canal, sphenoid
dis.tempting: Sphenoid disease is dangerous and sits against the orbital apex.
dis.ruled: Rare in children, and it would show apical signs before medial restriction.

items.q: He is admitted on intravenous antibiotics. Which change over 18 hours most supports drainage?

options.t: Temperature settles after two doses while the lid oedema persists
CT shows a 4 mm medial subperiosteal collection, acuity improving
Acuity falls to 20/80 with worse colour and an abscess crowding the apex
Blood cultures grow an organism fully sensitive to current therapy
Chemosis increases while pupil, colour and acuity stay unchanged

items.short: Falling function with an apical abscess
items.why: Drainage is driven by function and location, not by the presence of a collection. Falling afferent function with apical involvement is the indication, as is failure to improve on adequate therapy.

dis.label: Abscess, function improving
dis.tempting: An abscess on imaging feels like a surgical finding by definition.
dis.ruled: Small medial collections often resolve on antibiotics. Imaging does not decide.

dis.label: Chemosis increasing
dis.tempting: It looks like deterioration in front of you.
dis.ruled: Surface swelling with unchanged afferent function is no reason to open an orbit.

rules: If lid swelling comes with any change in acuity, colour, pupil, motility or globe position, treat it as orbital until imaging says otherwise. If function falls, drain.

rows: Crosses to the other eye within hours to days
Motility limited by swelling and pain
III, IV, VI and V1-V2 out of proportion to swelling
RAPD if the apex is crowded
RAPD plus a poorly reactive mid-dilated pupil
pair.decider: Bilateral signs, or multiple cranial neuropathies out of proportion to orbital swelling, mean cavernous sinus and neurosurgical admission rather than orbital drainage.
